Ordnance Survey 2026","caption":null},{"id":"84645","title":"Conformal Projections","subtitle":undefined,"text":"\u003Cp\u003EThe projection often used for maps of the world (rightly or wrongly &ndash; you decide) is the Mercator projection, created by Gerhard Mercator in 1569. This projection was designed to represent sailing courses of constant bearing (rhumb lines) as straight lines. This is a conformal projection which projection preserves angles and means that a straight line drawn on a map between two locations represents a line of constant bearing i.e. measure the angle on the map, set your compass and off you go.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EIt is still used to this day for maritime and air charts. It does however distort areas and distances and this distortion increases toward the poles. On a Mercator projection, Greenland and Africa appear to be a similar size, however Africa is approximately 14 times larger than Greenland. Not a great projection to use if you want to represent the relative areas of countries correctly.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E","link":null,"linkButtonLevel":"secondary","media":{"type":"image","value":{"id":"659a7885-9aca-447d-8394-130546720f42","aspectRatio":1,"assetWidth":1080,"assetHeight":1080,"transformations":null,"caption":null,"imageNextProps":{"src":"\u002Fimg-assets\u002Fmedia-components\u002Fcartoweek-mapprojections-1.x18a4f33b.png","alt":"","width":1080,"height":1080,"sizes":"100vw"},"copyrightNotice":undefined}},"imagePosition":"end","headingLevel":2,"layout":"One column switch","copyrightNotice":undefined,"caption":null},{"id":"84646","title":"Equal Area Projection","subtitle":undefined,"text":"\u003Cp\u003EEqual area projections are commonly used for mapping distributions such as population density, land cover, or climatic regions. When mapping distributions it is important that the relative areas of different regions or countries are presented correctly. Equal area projections however distort shapes, angles, and distances. Examples of equal area projections include Albers Equal Area Conic, Equal Earth, Gall-Peters, Mollweide, and Eckert IV. The distortion to shape can however make some areas look unrecognisable. If you look at the little circles on the Albers Equal Area Conic Projection, you can see their shape is preserved well in mid Northern latitudes. As such, this projection is often used for maps of Europe.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E","link":null,"linkButtonLevel":"secondary","media":{"type":"image","value":{"id":"90ad7358-2fe8-475d-b7eb-cd31d2767590","aspectRatio":1.000925925925926,"assetWidth":1081,"assetHeight":1080,"transformations":null,"caption":null,"imageNextProps":{"src":"\u002Fimg-assets\u002Fmedia-components\u002Fcartoweek-mapprojections-2.xf7d1a6a5.png","alt":"","width":1081,"height":1080,"sizes":"100vw"},"copyrightNotice":undefined}},"imagePosition":"start","headingLevel":2,"layout":"One column switch","copyrightNotice":undefined,"caption":null}],"layout":"One column switch"},"gridTile":{"width":undefined,"headingLevel":null,"boxed":undefined}},{"id":"84647","fieldName":"imageFlexible","value":{"id":"0d16c917-de5c-44a3-88ee-ee5fdec8d80d","aspectRatio":1.000925925925926,"assetWidth":1081,"assetHeight":1080,"transformations":null,"caption":null,"imageNextProps":{"src":"\u002Fimg-assets\u002Fmedia-components\u002Fcartoweek-mapprojections-4.x25c67f40.png","alt":"Equal earth projection map","width":1081,"height":1080,"sizes":"100vw"},"copyrightNotice":undefined,"layout":"Aligned centred"},"gridTile":{"width":undefined,"headingLevel":undefined,"boxed":undefined}},{"id":"84648","fieldName":"articleImageTextBlock","value":{"articleImagesTexts":[{"id":"84649","title":"Equidistant projection","subtitle":undefined,"text":"\u003Cp\u003EEquidistant projections do as they say, they preserve distances and therefore should be used if representing the distance between two points correctly is important to the purpose of the map. Most equidistant maps preserve scale along one or more lines or between two other points on the map. No projection can preserve all distances. One type of equidistant projection is an azimuthal equidistant projection which preserves distance from a single specified point on the projection and any other point on the map and is often used to map the polar regions.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E","link":null,"linkButtonLevel":"secondary","media":{"type":"image","value":{"id":"03b52330-8e41-4bde-9692-1b041e89d83a","aspectRatio":1.000925925925926,"assetWidth":1081,"assetHeight":1080,"transformations":null,"caption":null,"imageNextProps":{"src":"\u002Fimg-assets\u002Fmedia-components\u002Fcartoweek-mapprojections-5.x0abce8aa.png","alt":"","width":1081,"height":1080,"sizes":"100vw"},"copyrightNotice":undefined}},"imagePosition":"start","headingLevel":2,"layout":"One column","copyrightNotice":undefined,"caption":null}],"layout":"One column"},"gridTile":{"width":undefined,"headingLevel":null,"boxed":undefined}},{"id":"84650","fieldName":"text","value":{"text":"\u003Ch2\u003E7. Cartographic Design\u003C\u002Fh2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EWith the release of open data and a boom in the open-source industry, more people than ever before are delving into the world of cartography. Maps are becoming widely adopted by technologies and services as a form of data visualisation, by people who may not have come from a traditional mapping background. Too often a good idea might be let down by the poor application of cartographic techniques.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EAt Ordnance Survey, we have a dedicated Geographic Data Visualisation (GDV) team who specialise in creating great maps and data visualisations. As a team we have come up with some design principles which we believe lead to better map design. These are explained in detail in our \u003Ca href=\"https:\u002F\u002Fgithub.com\u002FOrdnanceSurvey\u002FGeoDataViz-Toolkit\"\u003EGeoDataViz Toolkit\u003C\u002Fa\u003E along with a load of other useful resources to help you create great maps.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Ch3\u003EOrdnance Survey&rsquo;s eight principles of cartographic design\u003C\u002Fh3\u003E\n\u003Ch4\u003EUnderstanding user requirements\u003C\u002Fh4\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EFully understanding the requirements of the user is vital to the success of any map! An effectively designed map is one in which the intended message is clearly communicated to the map user. This is only possible by fully understanding what that message is and how the map is intended to be used.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EBefore you start designing your map, ask the following questions:\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EWhat information does the map user require?\u003C\u002Fli\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EHow will they use the map?\u003C\u002Fli\u003E\n\u003C\u002Ful\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EKeep asking these questions throughout the map design process. If you realise you have added something to your map that the user does not require, remove it! It will only result in distraction or cause confusion if it is kept.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Ch4\u003EConsideration of display format\u003C\u002Fh4\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ETo achieve maximum clarity a map should be designed from the very beginning with its final display medium in mind. Is it going to be viewed on a phone screen or a computer screen? Is it designed to be printed, and if so, what size will it be and under what lighting or environmental conditions will the map be used?\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EUnderstanding the display format will allow you to make decisions relating to the scale of the map, the colour mode (RGB for screen or CMYK for print), the minimum point size of text, the size of features, and the level of functionality or interactivity given to the user.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Ch4\u003EClear visual hierarchy\u003C\u002Fh4\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThe aim here is to draw attention to certain elements of the map and push those of less importance further down the visual plane - although certain features are less important, they may still be required to give context. If not, then they should be removed. This helps the user differentiate between map features and helps them comprehend the maps message effectively. Key to this is the contrast between the &lsquo;figure&rsquo; (the focus of the map) and the &lsquo;ground&rsquo; (background or contextual information). This can be achieved by adjusting the graphic variables discussed above in relation to symbology.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E"},"gridTile":{"width":undefined,"headingLevel":undefined,"boxed":undefined}},{"id":"84651","fieldName":"imageFlexible","value":{"id":"b3e1165b-d468-476c-ab73-ebb5ead78845","aspectRatio":1.7770597738287561,"assetWidth":1100,"assetHeight":619,"transformations":null,"caption":null,"imageNextProps":{"src":"\u002Fimg-assets\u002Fmedia-components\u002Fvisual-hierarchy.x185a09f8.jpg","alt":"Example of visual hierarchy","width":1100,"height":619,"sizes":"100vw"},"copyrightNotice":undefined,"layout":"Aligned centred"},"gridTile":{"width":undefined,"headingLevel":undefined,"boxed":undefined}},{"id":"84652","fieldName":"text","value":{"text":"\u003Ch4\u003ESimplicity\u003C\u002Fh4\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECartography aims to portray spatial information in an appropriate way in order to transform information into knowledge. The inclusion of unnecessary information makes this process less effective, and one should always assess that information&rsquo;s value to the user against map clutter and confusion.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Ch4\u003ELegibility\u003C\u002Fh4\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EAll map elements need to be legible, meaning that they are readable, understandable, and recognisable at the intended viewing scale, and on the media on which the final map will be displayed.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ELegibility of most map features depends on colour and size. Symbols need to be simple enough to be recognised and offer good contrast against the background and large enough to be visible, but not so large they clutter the map. To achieve legibility, the process of cartographic generalisation is often required.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Ch4\u003EConsistency\u003C\u002Fh4\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EConsistency provides a map with balance. It enables features to be perceived as being organised into groups and it allows maps themselves to belong to a family of products through a shared identity.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EConsistency leads to effective communication through the concept of familiarity. If the same symbol is used repeatedly to depict the same feature, then once the user understands what that symbol represents, they can recognise it immediately thereafter. Conversely, inconsistency can lead to confusion and poor communication of the map&rsquo;s intended message.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Ch4\u003EAccessibility\u003C\u002Fh4\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EMaking maps and making geographic data and accompanying stylesheets easily obtainable and usable is imperative to successful use. Accessibility factors to consider in the design process include distribution formats, user disabilities, cost, and intuitiveness in use.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EMany maps are now presented in an electronic format and thus it is important to ensure that the file formats and software required to view the map are accessible.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EGood maps should be designed with the user&rsquo;s ability in mind, and should be easy and intuitive to use. In addition, to be fully inclusive, attention should be paid to the colour pallets used and how they work for people with colour vision deficiency (CVD).\u003C\u002Fp\u003E"},"gridTile":{"width":undefined,"headingLevel":undefined,"boxed":undefined}},{"id":"84653","fieldName":"articleImageTextBlock","value":{"articleImagesTexts":[{"id":"84654","title":"Good Composition","subtitle":undefined,"text":"\u003Cp\u003EComposition concerns the arrangement of all the different parts of a map, from the map&rsquo;s title to the scale bar. It is both how the map is structured and positioned, and how the map works alongside any additional information. All elements of the map should work together to provide a clear and complete understanding to the user. Their style should also be harmonious or complementary and the composition as a whole should appear balanced.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThe aim here is to achieve balance but the &lsquo;visual path&rsquo; on which you take the user should also be considered.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E","link":null,"linkButtonLevel":"secondary","media":{"type":"image","value":{"id":"02da7dfc-af1e-4613-b137-23d4ac92217e","aspectRatio":1.1498470948012232,"assetWidth":1880,"assetHeight":1635,"transformations":null,"caption":null,"imageNextProps":{"src":"\u002Fimg-assets\u002Fmedia-components\u002Fqe-olympic-park.x55dfbdee.jpg","alt":"Example of good composition","width":1880,"height":1635,"sizes":"100vw"},"copyrightNotice":undefined}},"imagePosition":"start","headingLevel":2,"layout":"One column","copyrightNotice":undefined,"caption":null}],"layout":"One column"},"gridTile":{"width":undefined,"headingLevel":null,"boxed":undefined}},{"id":"84655","fieldName":"text","value":{"text":"\u003Cp\u003EThere is no right or wrong answer to how to create a good map and what works depends on your use case and data.
